newsitem.title: UK: EBRD urges Bulgaria to speed up economic reform.
newsitem.headline: EBRD urges Bulgaria to speed up economic reform.

text.p: The European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) on Tuesday warned Bulgaria to stick to promised economic reforms if the government wanted more of its help.

"We will have to pace any increase in our activities and country exposure in accordance with the success of the stabilisation and restructuring programme undertaken by the government," head of the bank's Bulgaria team, Olivier Descamps said in a statement.
The unusually harsh comments underline the pressure Bulgaria is facing from the international community to fix its economy, about the worst performer in the old East Bloc.
The International Monetary Fund has twice delayed payment of part of a promised loan because Bulgaria has failed to meet economic targets.
The IMF is demanding Sofia curb inflation, stabilise its currency, shut dozens of loss-making state firms and accelearte privatisation.

The EBRD, set up six years ago to promote the private sector as eastern Europe switches to capitalism, said the key problems were delay in state sector structural reform, an ineffective banking system, and a reluctance to turn companies over to private hands.
"These adverse conditions are partly due to a lack of corporate governance, with local interests and corruption deterring the urgently needed reforms.
"Urgent measures would be needed to eliminate these obstacles and the Bank would support the efforts of the government in this direction," it said.
A Bank spokeswoman said there was no question of the EBRD pulling out of Bulgaria.
"We want to do as many projects as we can, as long as they abide by our conditions," she said.
The Bank has revised its strategy for Bulgaria to take into account the current critical economic situation.

Over the next two years it will focus on support for private sector development through cash and mass privatisation, strengthening of the ailing banking sector and support for development of critical infrastructure.
Only 18 percent of the projects the Bank has signed with Bulgaria have been in the private sector, far below the 60 percent it is supposed to reach by the middle of next year.
